definition: GitHub's CI/CD and automation service. Workflows in .github/workflows/ run jobs on runners, and each job's steps run commands or use actions - reusable building blocks from GitHub's marketplace, such as azure/login and azure/webapps-deploy. Workflows are privileged code: least-privilege tokens, pinned actions and reviewed changes.
example: The shop-api workflow builds once, deploys to staging, and swaps to production after an operations review.

definition: A YAML file in .github/workflows/ that defines triggers (push, pull request, manual, schedule), jobs that run in parallel unless ordered with needs, and steps. Top-level permissions set what the GITHUB_TOKEN can do; concurrency groups stop overlapping deployments.
example: .github/workflows/deploy.yml runs on pushes to main with contents: read by default and id-token: write only in deploy jobs.

definition: The machine that runs a GitHub Actions job. GitHub-hosted runners are fresh VMs per job; larger runners add capacity, static IPs and Azure private networking; self-hosted runners run on your own machines or Kubernetes. Windows minutes count double and macOS ten times. Never attach self-hosted runners to public repositories.
example: The API builds on ubuntu-latest; the iOS app builds on a macOS runner, which uses minutes ten times faster.

definition: A workflow that other workflows call with workflow_call, so build and deploy logic lives in one place - typically a platform repository - instead of being copied. Composite actions package groups of steps; organisation rulesets can require specific workflows on every repository.
example: shop-web, shop-api and shop-infra all call the deploy workflow in shop/platform.

definition: A named deployment target in a GitHub repository with its own variables and secrets and protection rules - required reviewers, allowed deployment branches or tags, wait timers and custom checks - that must pass before a job using it runs. Binding each Azure federated identity to an environment keeps production credentials out of every other job.
example: The production environment requires an operations reviewer and only accepts deployments from main.
